svg.aria-label: Diagram: how dynamic routing mode is a single per-network setting that governs every Cloud Router in the VPC network and acts in both directions at once, deciding both which learned routes reach which regions and which subnet routes are advertised outward; the regional mode where each region processes only its own BGP tasks so dynamic routes have next hops within that region alone; the global mode where each region also publishes its lowest-MED best path to every other region and an inter-regional cost unique to each region pair is added to the MED, with the own-region cost being zero; the two control planes where the dynamic route control plane selects and truncates before the VPC control plane may still suppress a candidate; and the scope limit that the mode governs Cloud Routers only and not policy-based or route-based VPN tunnels
svg.title: Dynamic routing mode: one network-wide switch that works in both directions and expresses distance as MED
svg.text: One setting on the network, not the router — and it works in both directions at once.
It decides what you learn from peers AND what you advertise to them. Most readings cover half.
The two modes, as the documentation defines them
REGIONAL: each region’s dynamic route control plane processes learned routes ONLY from the
Cloud Router BGP tasks IN ITS OWN REGION. Resulting routes have next hops in that region only.
GLOBAL: each region ALSO sends the best path for each prefix to every other region in use.
Resulting routes can have next hops in ANY region.
One associated mode per VPC network, controlling the behaviour of ALL of its Cloud Routers.
It is bidirectional, and the outbound half is the one people miss
INBOUND: whether routes learned from the peer apply in the tunnel’s region only, or in all.
OUTBOUND: whether subnet routes from ONLY the tunnel’s region, or from ALL regions, are
shared with your peer router or gateway.
So flipping to global does not merely widen what you can reach — it widens what your peer
is told about you. A peer with a tight prefix limit may notice before you do.
Distance is expressed as MED, and the cost is per region PAIR
Advertised MED for SAME-region subnet ranges = the BGP session’s configured base priority.
For OTHER regions = base priority PLUS an inter-regional cost.
Own-region inter-regional cost is 0. Other regions’ costs are NONZERO and UNIQUE TO EACH
REGION PAIR — sending region and receiving region. The values are not published.
Custom advertised ranges are exempt: the mode has NO effect on their advertised MED.
Two control planes, two chances to lose a route
The DYNAMIC ROUTE control plane selects, adds inter-regional cost, sorts by MED and
TRUNCATES — guaranteeing only that the LOWEST-MED routes reach the next stage.
In global mode it also removes every next hop except those with the SMALLEST inter-regional
cost — which is what makes a local path win over a remote one.
The VPC control plane may then still SUPPRESS a candidate — most often because its prefix
conflicts with a local, peering or NCC subnet route.
Where the setting does and does not reach
IT ONLY AFFECTS CLOUD ROUTERS. It does NOT affect Cloud VPN policy-based or route-based
tunnels — so a Classic VPN estate can be unaffected by a change that looks network-wide.
It DOES reach outward: with peering, the mode of the network that EXPORTS custom routes
controls how dynamic routes are created in the peers that import them.
And NCC dynamic routes follow the mode of the network holding the HYBRID SPOKE, not yours.
Above all of it, unchanged by either mode: DYNAMIC ROUTES ALWAYS RANK BELOW STATIC ROUTES.
Global mode buys reach and failover. It does not buy precedence.
